title: She said that …
title_target: Lena sa att vi har prov om två veckor.
goal: Pass on what other people said and asked — *Hon sa att…*, *Han frågade om…*, *Hon undrade vad…* — with the word order of a subordinate clause.
bekal: you can report statements with *sa att* and keep *inte* before the verb
you can report yes/no questions with *om* and other questions with *vad, när, var, varför*
you can ask politely and indirectly: *Vet du när…?*, *Jag undrar om…*
wave: Go back to Unit 8: reread the sentences with *eftersom* and *för att*, then report three of them as if someone else had said them: *Hon sa att hon stannade hemma eftersom hon var sjuk.*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vad sa hon?
dialogs.intro: Nine o'clock on a Wednesday evening. Dian comes home from her Swedish evening class, tired. Elin is on the sofa with a book — and has news of her own.

lines.id: Hi! How was the evening class?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Bra, men lite stressig. Lena sa att vi har prov om två veckor.
lines.id: Good, but a bit stressful. Lena said we have a test in two weeks.
lines.literal: good, but little stressful. Lena said that we have test in two weeks.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Om två veckor? Sa hon vad provet handlar om?
lines.id: In two weeks? Did she say what the test is about?

notes: **Lena sa att…** — *sa* (**sah**) is the past of *säga* (to say). In formal writing you'll also see it spelled *sade*, but it's pronounced **sah** either way. After *sa att* comes an ordinary statement — but as a subordinate clause, so BIFF applies (see below).

**Sa hon vad provet handlar om?** — a question inside a sentence (an **indirect question**) keeps **statement** word order: *vad provet handlar om*, not *vad handlar provet om*. English does exactly the same: "what the test **is** about", not "what **is** the test about". *Handla om* (**HAHND-lah OM**) = to be about.

**Pablo frågade om vi får…** — a yes/no question has no question word, so Swedish reports it with **om** ("if, whether"): *Får vi ta med ett lexikon?* → *Pablo frågade **om** vi får ta med ett lexikon.* Same as English "asked **if** we could…".

**…att det inte går** and **…varför vi inte får** — the BIFF rule from Swedish 101, Unit 18, at work: in reported speech, *inte* jumps in front of the verb. Direct: *Det går **inte**.* Reported: *Lena sa att det **inte** går.* This is the single most common mistake in reported speech — watch it in every sentence.

**Jaså?** (**yah-SOH**) = "Oh really? Is that so?" — a small word of surprise or interest. **Stackars** (**STAHK-kahsh**, *rs* = "sh") = poor (as in pity) and never changes form: *stackars Pablo*, *stackars mig*, *stackars barnen*. **Det går inte** = it's not possible, it can't be done.

**Jo, hon trodde att du sov** — *jo* is the "yes" that contradicts a negative question (*Undrade hon **inte**…? — **Jo**!*). Note the tenses: when the reporting verb is in the past and the content is also past, both are past — *hon trodde att du sov*. **Sitta i skolbänken** (lit. "sit in the school bench") is an idiom for being back in school.

grammars.title: Reporting statements: sa att
body: Pronouns change just as in English (*jag* becomes *hon*, *ni* becomes *vi*). The word order becomes subordinate-clause order: subject first, and *inte* or other sentence adverbs **before** the verb.

head: What she said
What you report
rows: Lena sa att vi **har** prov om två veckor.
Han sa att han **aldrig kommer** i tid.
De sa att de **inte har** tid.

after: If what was said is still true, Swedish is happy to keep the present tense: *Lena sa att vi har prov om två veckor.* Swedes also often shift to the past (*Hon sa att hon var trött*) — you'll study that tense shift properly in Swedish 103.
Other reporting verbs follow the same pattern: *Hon skrev att…*, *Han svarade att…*, *Hon berättade att…*, *Jag tror att…*.

grammars.title: Reporting questions: om, vad, när, vem som
body: Yes/no questions are reported with **om**. Questions with a question word keep that word — and then switch to statement order.

head: Direct question
Reported question
rows: Pablo frågade **om** vi får använda lexikon.

after: The last two rows hide a trap: when *vem* or *vad* is itself the **subject** (who comes? what happened?), Swedish adds **som** in the reported question: *vem som kommer*, *vad som hände*. Without a subject of its own, the clause needs *som* to hold that slot — just like the relative *som* in Unit 13.
An indirect question doesn't get a question mark unless the whole sentence is a question: *Jag undrar när passet börjar.* — but *Vet du när passet börjar?*

blocks.text: Indirect questions are also the polite way to ask strangers for things. Wrapping your question in *Vet du…?*, *Kan du säga…?* or *Jag undrar…* softens it — just like English "Do you know where…?" instead of "Where is…?". Remember to switch to statement word order inside.

head: Direct (fine with friends)
Polite (fine with anyone)
rows: Kan du säga när bussen går?
Jag undrar om du är ledig på lördag.

blocks.title: Passing on a phone message
items: *Maja ringde och undrade om du kan jobba.* — Maja called and wondered if you can work.
*Hon sa att du kan ringa tillbaka ikväll.* — She said you can call back tonight.
*Hon frågade när du slutar kursen.* — She asked when you finish the course.
*Maja hälsar!* — Maja says hi!

blocks.text: Many newcomers to Sweden learn the language in free evening courses run by the municipality, often called SFI (*svenska för invandrare*, Swedish for immigrants). The classes are a world in miniature: an engineer from Syria next to a nurse from the Philippines and a student from Indonesia — all of them reporting to each other, in Swedish, what the teacher just said.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 13
items: The *som* in *vem som kommer* is a cousin of the relative *som* from Unit 13. Compare: *Mannen **som** kommer…* and *Jag vet inte vem **som** kommer.*
Report what you learned about the café's regulars: *Maja sa att Bengt kommer varje dag. Dian undrade vem som inte tycker om stamgästerna.*

vocab.en: to say hi, to send greetings
